title: Ramana at sixteen: who am I?
hookLine: a sixteen-year-old lies down on the floor as if dead, and asks what dies
carry: atman: the one the thoughts come to
tomorrow: how can someone work in the world and not get stained?

lines: HE LIES DOWN AS IF DEAD.
cards: Madurai, in south India, 1896. A schoolboy of sixteen named Venkataraman is alone in an upstairs room of his uncle's house. He isn't ill.

But, as he later told it, a sudden, overwhelming fear of death comes over him. He doesn't run for help. He lies down, stretches out stiff like a corpse, holds his breath, and asks himself: this body is dead.
They'll carry it to the burning ground. But am I dead?

teach.b: His answer, as he later told it, didn't come as an argument. The body lay still, and he felt himself fully alive, untouched by its death.

About six weeks later he left home for the holy hill of Arunachala, at Tiruvannamalai, and he stayed there the rest of his life. People came from everywhere to sit with him, and called him Ramana Maharshi.
His teaching was the question that boy asked on the floor: who am I? It is one of the oldest teachings in Hinduism, made small enough to carry.

teach.h: WHO AM I? ATMAN: THE SELF.
teach.b: The Upanishads call it atman: the Self, the one who sees, which is not the body and not the thoughts. In Advaita Vedanta, the school Ramana's teaching is usually placed in, atman is one with Brahman.
His short text Who Am I? turns it into a practice, self-inquiry. Thoughts will keep coming. Don't chase them, and don't fight them.
When one arrives, ask: to whom has this come?
To me. Then: who am I? The mind, he says, turns back toward its source, and the thought falls quiet.
In the end the questioning itself burns up, like the stick used to stir a funeral fire. The question isn't a riddle with an answer like I am this body.
It turns attention around, from what appears to the one it appears to.

The other modern teachers carried old paths into new rooms too: Vivekananda opened in Chicago with "Sisters and Brothers of America"; Gandhi read the Gita as a guide to action; Tagore made prayer into Gitanjali.
Ramana carried it into one question.

how: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry by asking "who am I?" whenever thoughts arise, in sitting practice and in daily life, and many visit his ashram at Arunachala in Tiruvannamalai; Vivekananda's addresses and Tagore's Gitanjali are read and recited widely.

o: the sage whose path fits in one question: who am I?
the poet who wrote Gitanjali as song offerings
the monk who spoke to a Chicago hall in English

games.q: the modern teachers — tap the pairs.
p: the Self: not the body, not the thoughts

s: Ramana's question wants a clever answer, like your name or your job
he says answers like 'I am this body' don't finish it; the question turns attention back to its source.
at sixteen, Ramana lay down as if dead and asked whether he died with the body
as he later told it, he found himself untouched by the body's death, and soon left for Arunachala.
in Who Am I?, Ramana says to fight each thought until it leaves
he says to ask to whom the thought came; the mind turns back and the thought falls quiet.

games.q: you're sitting with Ramana's question, and a thought about tomorrow's meeting shows up. what does Who Am I? suggest?
o: follow it and plan the meeting.
ask: to whom did this thought come?
push it away and try again.
games.why: ask to whom it came: to me. then, who am I? the questioning itself, Ramana says, is like the stick that stirs a funeral fire and is burned up in the end.

practice: Let the breath settle, and when a thought arrives, neither follow it nor push it away; ask quietly, to whom did this come? To me. Then ask, who am I?
Don't answer in words: let attention turn back toward the one who is asking, and rest there until the next thought comes.

wordCard.voice: Ramana. The boy of sixteen who asked what dies, and whose whole path fits in one question: who am I?

orig.note: Tamil, in Tamil script: nan yar, who am I? Ramana's question, the name of his short text.

carryVoice: Your line: atman: the one the thoughts come to. Tomorrow, a lotus leaf. Back tomorrow, same hill.
